summary: The paper builds a fully synthetic 'capital city' QA task with known ground-truth ambiguity (deterministic, ambiguous, and OOD countries) and trains a tiny (~0.4M-parameter) Transformer from scratch to test, in a controlled setting, whether semantic-clustering entropy beats lexical entropy at detecting ambiguity and whether a length-entropy confound exists. It reports two null/contrary results (lexical entropy matches or beats oracle semantic entropy at AUROC across three temperatures; no length confound appears) and one positive result (entropy and unmapped-token rate rise sharply on OOD questions). I re-ran the provided experiment.py end-to-end and confirmed every number in the paper (AUROC 1.000/0.965, group-wise mean entropies, length correlations, temperature ablation, final loss) reproduces exactly bit-for-bit, so the reported results are not overclaimed relative to what the code actually produces.
strengths:
- Full reproducibility: I reran experiment.py from scratch and every number in the Results tables (AUROC 1.000 vs 0.9648, length correlations -0.0086/-0.0575, per-group mean entropies, temperature ablation, final loss 0.8864) matched the paper and results.json exactly, which is rare and commendable for a submitted paper.
- The experimental design is genuinely appropriate for the narrow question asked: it isolates the lexical-vs-semantic comparison from the two real confounds (unknown ground truth, imperfect NLI clustering) that make this comparison intractable on real LLMs, by construction giving exact ground-truth ambiguity and an exact oracle semantic map.
- The paper is honest and well-calibrated about its own limitations (single seed, toy scale, alias mechanism only a narrow proxy for real paraphrase diversity, K=40 sample-count bound) and explicitly does not over-generalize the null length-confound result to real autoregressive generation, correctly noting the compounding-error mechanism isn't represented.
weaknesses:
- Single random seed for the entire study (explicitly acknowledged in Limitations): with only 25 deterministic and 25 ambiguous countries and one seed, there is no variance estimate on the AUROC or correlation numbers, so 'lexical >= semantic across three temperatures' is a single-draw comparison, not a statistically supported claim — a handful of reruns with different seeds (cheap, ~20s each on CPU) would have been feasible and were not done despite the paper noting 'CPU, minutes-scale study' repeatedly.
- The core mechanism explaining the null result (alias-choice entropy as a 'near-constant additive offset,' ≈ln 2) is a direct, almost tautological consequence of the design choice of exactly 2 aliases per city drawn independently of class — the paper acknowledges this in Discussion, but the framing in the Abstract and Conclusion ('contrary to the standard narrative') risks reading as a stronger update against semantic entropy than the mechanism supports; the effect is a designed-in property of the alias generator, not an emergent finding about semantic vs. lexical entropy in general.
- No comparison against real semantic-entropy implementations (NLI-clustering, not just the oracle map) even in the synthetic world — the paper only ever tests the oracle clustering, so the ecological validity of the 'semantic entropy' being compared to the literature's actual method (which incurs NLI-model error, unlike here) is limited; this is a reasonable scope choice but narrows the paper's relevance to the motivating literature more than the title/abstract convey.
- OOD results (section 4d) are presented as clean support for entropy-based epistemic-uncertainty detection, but no AUROC or quantitative separability metric is given for OOD vs. in-distribution (only mean entropy/unmapped-rate deltas), unlike the careful AUROC treatment given to the ambiguity-detection claims — this is an inconsistency in rigor within the same results section.
questions:
1. With the pipeline running in ~20 seconds on CPU, why not report results over multiple seeds (e.g., 5-10 reruns) to give the AUROC and correlation numbers any variance estimate, especially since the headline claim is a comparison of two numbers (1.000 vs 0.965) that could plausibly be within noise for a 25-vs-25 sample AUROC?
2. Did you test a version of the synthetic world with more than 2 aliases per city, or aliases whose length/count correlates with city identity (rather than being drawn independently), to see whether the 'additive offset' mechanism you propose actually breaks down once alias diversity is class-correlated — this seems like the direct test of your own explanation for the null result?
3. Can you provide an AUROC or other quantitative separability measure for the OOD vs. in-distribution comparison in Section 4(d), analogous to what's done for the ambiguity-detection results, so the OOD claim is on the same evidentiary footing as the main results?
